note.value: Ten of the colours and the pH each stands at are one supplier’s, from a figure for red cabbage indicator that runs from pH 2 to pH 11–12. The figure has nothing below 2 or above 12: red at pH 1 and yellow at pH 13 are from a table for the dyes of this family in general. Where one colour ends and the next begins is the model’s own.

low.working: 5 g of ammonia in 100 mL is 2.94 mol/L (17.0305 g/mol); one part in 20 of that is 0.147 mol/L. With pKb 4.75, pOH = (4.75 − log 0.147) ÷ 2 = 2.79, and pH = 14 − 2.79 = 11.21, which is 11.2 to a tenth.

high.working: 10 g of ammonia in 100 mL is 5.87 mol/L (17.0305 g/mol); one part in 20 of that is 0.294 mol/L. With pKb 4.75, pOH = (4.75 − log 0.294) ÷ 2 = 2.64, and pH = 14 − 2.64 = 11.36, which is 11.4 to a tenth.

note.value: This range is worked out, not measured. A public health agency gives household ammonia as 5 to 10% ammonia; at one part in twenty in water, the base constant of ammonia puts that at pH 11.2 to 11.4.

low.working: 5 g of sodium hypochlorite in 100 mL is 0.672 mol/L (74.44 g/mol); one part in 100 of that is 0.00672 mol/L. The pKb of hypochlorite is 14 − 7.40 = 6.60; with it, pOH = (6.60 − log 0.00672) ÷ 2 = 4.39, and pH = 14 − 4.39 = 9.61, which is 9.6 to a tenth.

high.working: 12.5 g of sodium hypochlorite in 100 mL is 1.68 mol/L (74.44 g/mol); one part in 100 of that is 0.0168 mol/L. The pKb of hypochlorite is 14 − 7.40 = 6.60; with it, pOH = (6.60 − log 0.0168) ÷ 2 = 4.19, and pH = 14 − 4.19 = 9.81, which is 9.8 to a tenth.

note.value: Bleach destroys the dye: the colour goes, so the indicator cannot say. The meter still reads it. Worked out, not measured, for sodium hypochlorite alone: bleach of 5 to 12.5%, at one part in a hundred, comes to pH 9.6 to 9.8.

low.working: 1.00 g of sodium hydroxide in 100 mL is 0.25 mol/L (39.997 g/mol); one part in 20 of that is 0.0125 mol/L. All of it gives hydroxide ions, so pH = 14 + log 0.0125 = 12.10, which is 12.1 to a tenth.

high.working: 5.00 g of sodium hydroxide in 100 mL is 1.25 mol/L (39.997 g/mol); one part in 20 of that is 0.0625 mol/L. All of it gives hydroxide ions, so pH = 14 + log 0.0625 = 12.80, which is 12.8 to a tenth.

note.value: Worked out, not measured, for sodium hydroxide in water alone: 1 to 5%, as one maker’s sheet gives, at one part in twenty comes to pH 12.1 to 12.8. That maker’s drain cleaner also holds bleach, which would take the colour out; this lab’s is taken to hold none.

note.value: Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate. A supplier’s sheet gives a 5% solution of it a pH of 5 to 8.2: it can read a little to either side of neutral.

sharedNote.value: Nothing on a laboratory bench is tasted: not a food, and not a medicine. This is sold under its maker’s own label, which gives its cautions; read that label. Eye protection is worn at this bench as at any other.
sharedNote.rationale: The one note that the foods, the toiletries, the medicines, the laundry detergent and the buffers from pH 2 to pH 12 share (spec 21.4). It is the lab's own and rests on no document: makers' labels differ, and the lab cannot know whose product is on a bench.

notes.value: The rack is your scale: one dye, a different colour at each step from strong acid to strong base. Acid gives the reds and pinks, neutral the blues, base the greens and yellows.
The pH 11 and pH 12 tubes look the same: the supplier’s figure gives one colour for both. There the indicator can place a sample only to within those two.
An indicator places a thing on the scale to about a unit. The meter reads to a tenth, but only from a probe that has been rinsed.
Bleach is the one thing the indicator could not place: it took the colour out.
One unit of pH is ten times in hydrogen ion, two units are a hundred times, and three a thousand. The lower the pH, the more hydrogen ion.

colourEdgesTenths.rationale: The highest pH, in tenths, that shows each colour but the last, in the table's order: the edges between neighbouring colours. They are the model's own. A source gives a colour for a pH or for a range, never the pH where one colour gives way to the next, so each edge is put half way between the two pH values named, and a sample exactly half way shows the lower colour. The last edge is the exception: the supplier's figure ends its greenish-yellow at 12, the other table has yellow at 13, and nothing read says what is seen between. The model shows yellow for everything above 12.0, so that the two tubes that share greenish-yellow, pH 11 and pH 12, are both within a unit of every sample of that colour.

oneInTwenty.rationale: The ammonia, the shampoo, the conditioner, the two detergents, the mouthwash and the drain cleaner are on the bench at about one part in twenty in water, as the directions have them. The model takes it as exactly twenty where it works a pH out.

oneInHundred.rationale: The bleach is on the bench at about one part in a hundred in water, as the directions have it. The model takes it as exactly a hundred where it works the pH out.

gramsPerHundredMillilitres.rationale: The antacid tablets, the aspirin and the Epsom salt are on the bench at about 5 g in 100 mL of water, as the directions have them. The tablets do not all dissolve.

productDensity.rationale: In grams per millilitre. Where a pH is worked out from a strength given in per cent, the per cent is taken as grams in 100 mL of the product: its density is taken as that of water. No density was read from a source. A product a tenth denser than water would read about 0.04 of a pH unit higher at the most.

dilutedReadsAsSold.rationale: 1 for yes. The sheets read for the shampoo, the conditioner and the mouthwash give a pH for the product as sold, and the bench has each at one part in twenty in water. The model takes the diluted sample to read inside the sheet's range. That is the lab's own: a product that holds a buffer keeps its pH on dilution, and one that does not moves toward 7. No source was read for it.

endBufferMolarity.rationale: In mol/L. The pH 1 buffer is taken as about 0.13 mol/L in hydrochloric acid and the pH 13 buffer as about 0.13 mol/L in sodium hydroxide, each with potassium chloride. The directions give no recipe; the figure is used only to choose which safety data sheet covers each, and no pH is worked out from it.

unrinsedSharePercent.rationale: What a probe that was not rinsed reads: the sample's own pH moved this share of the way toward the pH of the sample the probe was last in, to the nearest tenth. It is the model's own, with no source: a real probe carries over an amount that depends on how much liquid clings to it and on what both samples hold. The share is chosen to be large enough to see on the meter and small enough to be believed.

estimateWithinTenths.rationale: An estimate by eye counts when it is within one unit of the reading of a rinsed probe (spec 21.2).

neededToCount.rationale: The second part is done when eight of the household things count (spec 21.1); the rest are there to try.

sampleMicrolitres.rationale: A sample or a buffer in its tube is taken as 3 mL, so that a tube can be drawn to its level. Nothing is worked out from it.

indicatorMicrolitres.rationale: The indicator added to a tube is taken as ten drops, 0.5 mL, so that the tube is drawn a little fuller once it is in. Nothing is worked out from it.
